lead: A gear tooth does not see one fixed load for its whole life. It sees a load spectrum: full load in the morning, part load at night, shocks at starting. The tooth collects fatigue damage cycle by cycle. Gear life design turns that spectrum into one equivalent load, sizes the gears, then checks shafts, bearings, heat and lubrication. The same method sizes a gearbox for a textile mill, a crane or an electric vehicle reducer.
prereq: You need: spur gear design, helical gear design, fatigue S-N and Miner rule from Unit 2, and bearing life and lubrication from Unit 5.

blocks.text: Gear life is counted in load cycles on one tooth. A gear running at n rpm for L<sub>h</sub> hours gives N = 60 n L<sub>h</sub> cycles. A gear at 1200 rpm for 8,000 h sees 5.76×10<sup>8</sup> cycles.

blocks.where: n is gear speed in rpm; L<sub>h</sub> is design life in hours; N is load cycles on one tooth.

blocks.text: The S-N curve plots alternating stress S against cycles to failure N. On log-log axes it falls with a slope; for steel it becomes flat below the endurance limit S<sub>e</sub>. Bending fatigue and contact fatigue have separate S-N curves, because one starts at the tooth root and the other at the tooth surface.

Miner's rule adds damage fractions: D = Σ n<sub>i</sub> / N<sub>i</sub> ≤ 1. n<sub>i</sub> is cycles at stress level i; N<sub>i</sub> is cycles to failure at that stress from the S-N curve. D reaches 1 at predicted failure. Use D below 1 for reliability; a reliability factor raises the required size.
Design life in hours comes from the customer: 10,000 h for a workshop hoist, more for a power plant. Convert every duty point to cycles before comparing.

A load spectrum lists power P<sub>i</sub> or torque T<sub>i</sub> and the fraction of life p<sub>i</sub> at that level. For contact fatigue the equivalent power is P<sub>eq</sub> = (Σ p<sub>i</sub> P<sub>i</sub><sup>3</sup>)<sup>1/3</sup>. P<sub>i</sub> is power in kW; p<sub>i</sub> is a fraction that sums to 1; the exponent 3 comes from the contact S-N slope. The result is the steady power that gives the same contact damage as the spectrum. Some syllabi call it the cubic mean load.

blocks.where: P<sub>eq</sub> is equivalent contact power in kW; P<sub>i</sub> is power at duty point i in kW; p<sub>i</sub> is the fraction of life at that point.

blocks.text: For a torque spectrum replace P<sub>i</sub> by T<sub>i</sub>. For bending fatigue the exponent is different, so do not use the contact equivalent load for a bending check unless the same exponent applies. Apply a service factor K<sub>s</sub> to the nominal equivalent load: P<sub>design</sub> = K<sub>s</sub> P<sub>eq</sub>. K<sub>s</sub> accounts for shock, starting, reversing and application severity; it is selected from the application, not from the gear.

Do not use the maximum load for the whole life. That over-sizes and hides bearing or heat limits. Do not use the arithmetic average either; it under-sizes because damage grows with the cube of contact load.

A single-stage gearbox is simple and efficient; it suits ratios up to about 4 to 6. A two-stage gearbox splits the total ratio i into i = i<sub>1</sub> i<sub>2</sub>. Equal split i<sub>1</sub> = i<sub>2</sub> = √i keeps the stages similar in size. More stages add losses and cost, so use them only when the ratio or package needs it.

The housing carries bearing bores, holds oil and conducts heat to the air. It is ribbed for stiffness. Oil level reaches the lowest gear so splash lubrication works at moderate speed. At high speed use forced lubrication with a pump and oil cooler. Seals at the shafts keep oil in and dirt out; a breather stops pressure build-up.

blocks.where: ΔT is oil-to-air temperature rise in K; P<sub>in</sub> is input power in W; η is efficiency; h is heat transfer coefficient in W/(m²K); A is housing area in m².

blocks.text: At steady state heat generated equals heat lost: P<sub>in</sub>(1 − η) = h A ΔT. If ΔT is too high, add fins, a fan or an oil cooler. Check bearings by their own life formula in Unit 5. A gearbox can fail first on bearing life, seal leakage or oil temperature, not tooth bending.

figure.caption: The load spectrum is reduced by Miner's rule to one equivalent load; that load sizes the gears, then shafts and bearings, then heat and lubrication, and finally the housing.

spec.title: Gearbox design flow
spec.aria: A flow chart moves from load spectrum to equivalent load, gear size, shafts and bearings, heat and lubrication, and housing.

examples.question: A gearbox runs at 1000 rpm for 10,000 h. It transmits 10 kW for 60% of the time, 6 kW for 30% and 2 kW for 10%. For contact fatigue take life exponent m = 3. Find the equivalent power and the total cycles on a gear tooth.
steps: P<sub>eq</sub> = 665.6<sup>1/3</sup> = ∛665.6 = 8.73 kW (cube root, not division by 3).
examples.answer: The equivalent power is 8.73 kW and the tooth sees 6.0×10⁸ cycles in 10,000 h.
examples.check:
P1 = 10.0
P2 = 6.0
P3 = 2.0
f1 = 0.6
f2 = 0.3
f3 = 0.1
m = 3
Peq = (f1 * P1**m + f2 * P2**m + f3 * P3**m) ** (1 / m)
rpm = 1000
hours = 10000
N = 60 * rpm * hours
print(round(Peq, 2))
print(int(N))

traps: Using the maximum power for the whole life over-sizes the gears and hides the real heat or bearing limit.
Using the arithmetic average power under-sizes contact fatigue; contact damage follows the cube of load.
Counting life in hours and forgetting speed: cycles N = 60 n L<sub>h</sub>.
Using the contact exponent 3 for a bending check without changing to the bending exponent.
Forgetting the service factor, or applying it after the gear size is fixed.

quiz.q: What is the endurance limit of a gear material?
quiz.a: The alternating stress below which the S-N curve becomes flat and fatigue life is treated as infinite.

quiz.q: Why is gear life counted in cycles rather than hours?
quiz.a: Fatigue damage depends on the number of load repetitions, not elapsed time. Speed changes cycles per hour: N = 60 n L<sub>h</sub>.

quiz.q: A gear at 2000 rpm for 5000 h has 8 kW for 50% and 4 kW for 50%. Take m = 3. Find P<sub>eq</sub> and cycles.
A gearbox passes tooth bending but oil temperature exceeds the limit. List checks and one fix.
quiz.a: Check efficiency, housing area, oil flow, bearing life and seal condition. One fix is to add an oil cooler, fins or a fan to raise heat loss.
K<sub>s</sub> = design load / nominal load. It accounts for shock, starting, reversing and application severity.

quiz.q: Why not use the maximum load for the whole life?
quiz.a: It over-sizes the gears, ignores the real load spectrum, and can hide bearing-life or heat limits that may fail first.

quiz.q: A two-stage gearbox has total ratio 20. Suggest a stage split and explain.
quiz.a: Use i<sub>1</sub> = i<sub>2</sub> = √20 = 4.47. Equal split keeps the two stages similar in size and load.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry gearboxes are rated with standards such as ISO and AGMA, measured field load spectra, and thermal network models. Oil analysis and vibration monitoring track pitting before failure. Electric vehicle reducers add motor torque ripple and noise constraints. Search next for gear rating standards, Miner rule, and gearbox thermal analysis.
